readNotes: Pilot (Nov 4 2026). Full text of all 12 chapters read before writing. Passages are ledger-free runs of chapter 1 (With the Samanas); distractors drawn only from chapters 0-1.

p1.text: Dead to himself, not to be a self any more, to find tranquility with an emptied heart, to be open to miracles in unselfish thoughts, that was his goal. Once all of my self was overcome and had died, once every desire and every urge was silent in the heart, then the ultimate part of me had to awake, the innermost of my being, which is no longer my self, the great secret.

p2.text: And Siddhartha's soul returned, had died, had decayed, was scattered as dust, had tasted the gloomy intoxication of the cycle, awaited in new thirst like a hunter in the gap, where he could escape from the cycle, where the end of the causes, where an eternity without suffering began. He killed his senses, he killed his memory, he slipped out of his self into thousands of other forms, was an animal, was carrion, was stone, was wood, was water, and awoke every time to find his old self again, sun or moon shone, was his self again, turned round in the cycle, felt thirst, overcame the thirst, felt new thirst.

p3.text: He went the way of self-denial by means of pain, through voluntarily suffering and overcoming pain, hunger, thirst, tiredness. He went the way of self-denial by means of meditation, through imagining the mind to be void of all conceptions. These and other ways he learned to go, a thousand times he left his self, for hours and days he remained in the non-self.

p4.text: And once again, another time, when Siddhartha left the forest together with Govinda, to beg for some food in the village for their brothers and teachers, Siddhartha began to speak and said: "What now, O Govinda, might we be on the right path? Might we get closer to enlightenment? Might we get closer to salvation?

p5.text: But the most important thing, the path of paths, we will not find." "If you only," spoke Govinda, "wouldn't speak such terrible words, Siddhartha! How could it be that among so many learned men, among so many Brahmins, among so many austere and venerable Samanas, among so many who are searching, so many who are eagerly trying, so many holy men, no one will find the path of paths?"

p6.text: After all, the world was sick, life was hard to bear—and behold, here a source seemed to spring forth, here a messenger seemed to call out, comforting, mild, full of noble promises. Everywhere where the rumour of Buddha was heard, everywhere in the lands of India, the young men listened up, felt a longing, felt hope, and among the Brahmins' sons of the towns and villages every pilgrim and stranger was welcome, when he brought news of him, the exalted one, the Sakyamuni.

p8.text: Speak, friend, wouldn't we want to go there too and listen to the teachings from the Buddha's mouth?" Quoth Siddhartha: "Always, O Govinda, I had thought, Govinda would stay with the Samanas, always I had believed his goal was to live to be sixty and seventy years of age and to keep on practising those feats and exercises, which are becoming a Samana.

p9.text: So now you, my faithful friend, want to take a new path and go there, where the Buddha spreads his teachings." Quoth Govinda: "You're mocking me. Mock me if you like, Siddhartha! But have you not also developed a desire, an eagerness, to hear these teachings? And have you not at one time said to me, you would not walk the path of the Samanas for much longer?"

p10.text: But let's do it, my dear, I am willing to listen to these teachings—though in my heart I believe that we've already tasted the best fruit of these teachings." Quoth Govinda: "Your willingness delights my heart. But tell me, how should this be possible? How should the Gotama's teachings, even before we have heard them, have already revealed their best fruit to us?" Quoth Siddhartha: "Let us eat this fruit and wait for the rest, O Govinda!

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha plans to return to his father once he has learned to fast.
Siddhartha hopes to become a respected teacher among the oldest Samanas and their students.
Siddhartha wants to find joy and sorrow more fully than he did at home.
Siddhartha hopes that by emptying himself of the self, something deeper in him will wake.
A.explanation: The passage names one goal: to be "empty," "dead to himself," so that "the innermost of my being" can awake. Becoming a respected teacher is never mentioned. Feeling joy and sorrow more fully reverses the text, which wants him empty of both. Returning to his father is not part of this goal; the passage looks only inward, not home.

A.prompt: According to the passage, how did Siddhartha practise self-denial by means of meditation?
options: By standing in the rainy season until he felt no cold at all
By repeating the holy verses of the Brahmins
By begging for food in the villages each day
By imagining the mind to be empty of all ideas
A.explanation: The passage says he went "the way of self-denial by means of meditation, through imagining the mind to be void of all conceptions," which the key restates. Standing in the rain belongs to the way of pain described elsewhere, not meditation. Begging is a daily duty, not a method of self-denial here. Repeating Brahmin verses is not mentioned in this passage at all.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "carrion" most nearly means
options: dead and rotting flesh
a heavy burden
a wild bird that hunts for food
an empty shell
A.explanation: The list "was an animal, was carrion, was stone, was wood" names things his soul became, and earlier in the chapter his soul enters a dead jackal, so "dead and rotting flesh" fits. A hunting bird would be another animal, not a decayed body. A burden and an empty shell do not match the sense of a dead body left to decay.

A.prompt: Siddhartha's questions in the passage suggest that he
options: doubts that their efforts are leading them anywhere
is sure they have already reached enlightenment together
wants Govinda to beg for food alone
fears that their teachers will punish them
A.explanation: Asking whether they are "on the right path" and whether they "get closer" to salvation shows doubt that their work is leading anywhere. Being sure of enlightenment contradicts the questioning tone. Nothing suggests he wants Govinda to beg alone; they are walking together. Fear of punishment by teachers is never raised; his worry is about the path, not the Samanas.

A.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Govinda believe about Siddhartha?
options: Siddhartha is angry that Govinda wants to leave.
Siddhartha also wishes to hear the Buddha's teachings.
Siddhartha wants to stay with the Samanas for many years.
Siddhartha has already met the Buddha in the village.
A.explanation: Govinda asks, "have you not also developed a desire, an eagerness, to hear these teachings?" which shows he believes Siddhartha shares the wish. Staying with the Samanas for years is the opposite of what Govinda recalls Siddhartha saying. Govinda, not Siddhartha, heard news in the village. Siddhartha teases rather than shows anger, and Govinda calls it mocking, not rage.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "You're mocking me. Mock me if you like, Siddhartha!"
"So now you, my faithful friend, want to take a new path and go there, where the Buddha spreads his teachings."
"But have you not also developed a desire, an eagerness, to hear these teachings?"
"And have you not at one time said to me, you would not walk the path of the Samanas for much longer?"
A.explanation: Only the question about "a desire, an eagerness, to hear these teachings" shows Govinda believes Siddhartha wants to hear the Buddha. The "new path" line is Siddhartha describing Govinda's wish, not Govinda's belief. "You're mocking me" shows Govinda notices the teasing but says nothing of Siddhartha's wish. The reminder about not staying long concerns leaving the Samanas, not hearing the teachings.

A.prompt: The list "was an animal, was carrion, was stone, was wood, was water" mainly serves to
options: explain why Siddhartha gave away his garments
describe the fields, hills and rivers around the Samanas' forest
name the foods the Samanas were allowed to eat
show how many different forms Siddhartha's soul passed into
A.explanation: The list follows "he slipped out of his self into thousands of other forms," so it shows the range of forms his soul entered. It is not a description of the forest landscape, since these are things he became, not things he saw. Stone and water are not foods. His garments are not discussed in this passage.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The Buddha sent messengers to every town in India.
Life in India became easy once the rumour spread.
News of the Buddha brought hope to people in a suffering world.
The Brahmins' sons refused to welcome any of the pilgrims and strangers.
A.explanation: The passage says the world "was sick" and that, wherever the rumour was heard, young men "felt a longing, felt hope," which the key sums up. The Brahmins' sons welcomed pilgrims, so refusal is wrong. The "messenger" only "seemed" to call out; no real messengers are sent. Life is called "hard to bear," not easy.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what puzzles Govinda about Siddhartha's remark?
options: How the teachings could show their best fruit before being heard
Where the Buddha will be teaching the next day
Why Siddhartha refuses to listen to the teachings of the Buddha at all
Whether the Samanas will let them both leave
A.explanation: Govinda asks how the teachings, "even before we have heard them," could "have already revealed their best fruit," which the key restates. Siddhartha says he is "willing to listen," so he does not refuse. The Buddha's location is not asked about here. Leaving the Samanas is not what Govinda questions in this passage; he questions the "fruit."

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "mocking" most nearly means
options: warning
teasing
copying
praising
A.explanation: Govinda says "You're mocking me" after Siddhartha pretends surprise that Govinda wants to leave, so the sense is light teasing. "Copying" is another meaning of mock, but Siddhartha is not imitating him. "Praising" is the opposite of the playful jab. "Warning" does not fit, since Siddhartha gives no caution, only an amused remark about his friend.

options: wants to stop searching for the path of paths
cannot believe that so many devoted seekers would all fail
agrees with Siddhartha that no Samana will ever reach the goal
thinks that Siddhartha should become a Brahmin
A.explanation: Govinda asks how it could be that among so many learned and holy men "no one will find the path of paths," showing disbelief that all could fail. He does not agree; he objects to "such terrible words." Becoming a Brahmin is not suggested. He wants the search to succeed, so he is not ready to stop searching.

A.prompt: The phrase "like a hunter in the gap" suggests that Siddhartha's soul
options: had become cruel toward other creatures
was chasing wild animals through the forest and the fields
waited watchfully for a chance to escape the cycle
was trapped forever with no way out
A.explanation: The simile compares his soul to a hunter waiting at a gap "where he could escape from the cycle," so it waits watchfully for an opening. He is not literally chasing animals. Cruelty is not the point of the comparison; patience and alertness are. "Trapped forever" contradicts the hope of escape that the gap stands for.

B.prompt: According to the passage, who was welcome among the Brahmins' sons of the towns and villages?
options: Teachers who could recite the holy verses
Only Samanas who had fasted for many days in the forest
Any pilgrim or stranger who brought news of the Buddha
Merchants who came to trade in the villages
B.explanation: The passage states that "every pilgrim and stranger was welcome, when he brought news of him," the Buddha, which the key restates. Samanas who fasted are not singled out. Merchants and trade are not mentioned in this passage. Teachers reciting verses are also absent; what made a visitor welcome was news of the Sakyamuni, not learning.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "rumour" most nearly means
options: report passed along by word of mouth
long poem
official order given by a king
loud noise
B.explanation: The "rumour of Buddha" is something "heard" in many lands and brought by pilgrims and strangers, so it is a report passed from person to person. A loud noise does not carry news about a person. An official order would come from a ruler, which the passage never mentions. A long poem does not fit how the news travels.

B.prompt: Siddhartha's words to Govinda in the passage suggest that he
options: expects the teachings themselves to add little to what he already has
refuses to make the journey unless Govinda goes first
believes Govinda has misunderstood the Buddha's teachings
is eager to become one of the Buddha's first and most faithful disciples
B.explanation: He is "willing to listen" but believes "we've already tasted the best fruit of these teachings," so he expects little more from the teachings. Eagerness to become a disciple overstates his guarded tone. He does not accuse Govinda of misunderstanding the teachings, which neither has heard. He says "let's do it," so he sets no condition about who goes first.

B.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Siddhartha believe will happen once his self is overcome?
options: He will no longer need to eat, drink or sleep at all.
A deeper, hidden part of his being will awaken.
He will be able to teach the other Samanas.
His old desires will return more strongly.
B.explanation: The passage says that once the self "had died," "the ultimate part of me had to awake, the innermost of my being," so a hidden part will wake. Needing no food or sleep is not stated as the result. Teaching others is never his goal here. The return of desire contradicts the hope that "every desire and every urge was silent."

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "to be open to miracles in unselfish thoughts"
"Dead to himself, not to be a self any more"
"then the ultimate part of me had to awake, the innermost of my being"
"Once all of my self was overcome and had died"
B.explanation: Only the line about "the ultimate part of me" having "to awake" states what Siddhartha expects to happen after the self is overcome. "Dead to himself" describes the goal of emptying, not its result. "Open to miracles" names a state he seeks, not the awakening. "Every desire... silent" is the condition that comes first, not the outcome.

B.prompt: The three questions at the end of the passage mainly serve to
options: list the duties the teachers have given the young men in the forest
describe the village where they go to beg
build a growing doubt about whether their path leads anywhere
show that Govinda has already answered Siddhartha
B.explanation: Each question ("on the right path," "closer to enlightenment," "closer to salvation") presses the same worry, building doubt about where their efforts lead. They are questions, not a list of duties. Govinda has not yet spoken in this passage, so nothing has been answered. The village is only where they beg; the questions say nothing about it.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha discovered that pain, not meditation, was the only true path to wisdom.
Siddhartha learned several ways of leaving the self, through pain and meditation.
Siddhartha taught the Samanas a new way of meditating.
Siddhartha gave up self-denial after a few hours.
B.explanation: The passage describes self-denial "by means of pain" and "by means of meditation," then "these and other ways," so it centres on learning several methods. Calling pain the only path ignores meditation. He learns from the Samanas; he does not teach them. He stayed "for hours and days" in the non-self, so he did not quit after a few hours.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "void" most nearly means
options: invalid
empty
dark
silent
B.explanation: "Imagining the mind to be void of all conceptions" means picturing the mind empty of ideas. "Invalid" is the legal sense of void (a void contract), which does not fit a mind. "Dark" and "silent" describe light and sound, but the phrase is about the mind containing no conceptions, so emptiness is the meaning.

B.prompt: Govinda's repeated phrase "among so many" mainly serves to
options: list the teachers Govinda wishes to leave behind
show that Govinda is unsure exactly how many Samanas, Brahmins and holy men there are
suggest that most seekers are only pretending
stress the great number of seekers, making Siddhartha's claim seem unlikely
B.explanation: Repeating "among so many" piles up learned men, Brahmins, Samanas and holy men, so the sheer number makes "no one will find" sound unlikely to Govinda. He is not unsure of a count; he is arguing. He names groups he respects, not teachers to leave. Calling them pretenders reverses his praise of "venerable" and "holy" men.

B.prompt: Siddhartha's reply in the passage implies that he had
options: assumed Govinda would remain with the Samanas for life
asked the Buddha to come and teach in the forest
known for many long years that Govinda wanted to see the Buddha
planned to leave Govinda behind with the Samanas
B.explanation: He says "always I had believed his goal was to live to be sixty and seventy" practising Samana exercises, so he assumed Govinda would stay for life. That rules out knowing all along that Govinda wanted to see the Buddha. No plan to leave Govinda is stated here. He never asked the Buddha to come to the forest.

B.prompt: The narrator's account in the passage is best described as
options: Siddhartha's own spoken account of his years with the Samanas, given to Govinda
a debate between the oldest Samana and Siddhartha
a summary of what the villagers said about the Samanas
a close report of Siddhartha's inner experience, told in the third person
B.explanation: The narrator describes from outside ("He killed his senses") yet reports what happens inside Siddhartha's soul, so it is a close third-person account. Siddhartha is not speaking; there are no quotation marks. No one debates, so there is no exchange with the oldest Samana. The villagers do not appear; the passage stays inside his experience.

B.prompt: How does Govinda's view in Passage 2 relate to the doubt Siddhartha voices in Passage 1?
options: Govinda accepts it but says that only the Brahmins will succeed.
Govinda shares it fully and adds several new reasons for both of them to leave the Samanas.
Govinda ignores it and talks instead about begging for food.
Govinda rejects it, arguing that so many devoted seekers cannot all fail.
B.explanation: In Passage 1 Siddhartha doubts they are "on the right path"; in Passage 2 Govinda calls his words "terrible" and asks how "no one" among so many could find the path, so he rejects the doubt. He does not share it or give reasons to leave. He answers directly rather than ignoring it. He never says only Brahmins succeed.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha finally broke free of the cycle for good by killing his senses.
The Samanas' exercises made Siddhartha forget his thirst for good.
Each escape from the self ended with Siddhartha back where he began.
Siddhartha preferred being an animal to being a man.
C.explanation: The passage moves through many forms but ends with him awaking "every time to find his old self again" and feeling "new thirst," so each escape returns him to the start. He did not break free; he "turned round in the cycle." No preference for animal life is stated. His thirst returns, so it is not forgotten for good.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that the news of the Buddha spread widely partly because
options: the Buddha himself travelled to every town in India
the Brahmins ordered every town and village in the land to repeat it
pilgrims were paid for each report they carried
people burdened by a hard life were ready to hope for relief
C.explanation: The passage links the spread to the state of the world: life "was hard to bear," and listeners "felt a longing, felt hope," so their need helped the news travel. No Brahmin order is described. The Buddha is not said to visit every town; the rumour travels instead. Pilgrims were "welcome," but nothing says they were paid.

C.prompt: The parallel sentences beginning "He went the way of self-denial by means of" mainly serve to
options: suggest that the Samanas disagreed about the right method
contrast a path Siddhartha chose with one he rejected after trying it
present pain and meditation as two routes toward the same aim
show that meditation is harder than enduring pain
C.explanation: Both sentences share the same opening and differ only in the means, pain or meditation, so they present two routes to one aim, leaving the self. He took both, so neither is rejected. The passage does not rank one as harder. No disagreement among Samanas is mentioned; the passage is about what Siddhartha himself learned.

C.prompt: Which choice best describes Siddhartha's attitude toward the journey to hear the Buddha?
options: Eager to go, because he expects the Buddha to give a final answer to his questions
Indifferent, because he thinks the trip is Govinda's concern only
Willing to go, but doubtful that the teachings will give much more
Unwilling to go, because he wants to remain a Samana
C.explanation: He says "let's do it" and is "willing to listen," yet believes they have "already tasted the best fruit," so he is willing but doubtful. Eagerness for a final answer ignores that doubt. He agrees to go, so he is not unwilling. He joins the plan and explains his view to Govinda, so he is not indifferent.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "though in my heart I believe that we've already tasted the best fruit of these teachings"
"How should the Gotama's teachings, even before we have heard them, have already revealed their best fruit to us?"
"Your willingness delights my heart."
"Let us eat this fruit and wait for the rest, O Govinda!"
C.explanation: The "though in my heart" line joins his willingness with his doubt, matching the answer. "Your willingness delights my heart" is Govinda's reaction, not Siddhartha's attitude. The "How should" line is Govinda's question. "Let us eat this fruit" shows willingness and patience but not his doubt about what the teachings will add.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "tranquility" most nearly means
options: calm
safety
sleep
silence
C.explanation: Siddhartha seeks "to find tranquility with an emptied heart," a state of inner calm with no desire stirring. "Silence" concerns sound, though the passage speaks of urges, not noise, being silent. "Safety" means freedom from danger, which is not his aim. "Sleep" is a loss of awareness, but he wants to be "open to miracles," fully awake.

C.prompt: The phrase "here a source seemed to spring forth" most likely presents the Buddha's teaching as
options: a danger rising up to threaten the Brahmins
a fresh spring that might relieve a thirsting, sick world
a riddle that the young men had to solve
the origin of every rumour and every story heard in the lands of India
C.explanation: A "source" that springs forth is water rising from the ground; set beside a world that "was sick," it suggests relief, like water for the thirsty, an image the book uses for Siddhartha's own thirst. It is not the source of every rumour. Nothing marks it as a danger to Brahmins. The young men feel hope, not puzzlement over a riddle.

C.prompt: Govinda's questions at the end of the passage imply that he thinks Siddhartha's teasing
options: shows Siddhartha has lost interest in teachings
proves that Siddhartha wants to stay behind
means Siddhartha is angry with the Buddha
hides a wish Siddhartha shares with him
C.explanation: Govinda answers the teasing by asking whether Siddhartha has "not also developed a desire" and recalling that he would not stay long, implying the mockery hides a shared wish. That rules out wanting to stay behind. Govinda assumes interest, not lost interest. Nothing suggests anger at the Buddha, whom neither has met; the friends speak only of each other.

C.prompt: The repetition of "always" in Siddhartha's reply mainly serves to
options: show that Govinda always agrees with whatever Siddhartha says and decides
stress how firmly he had held a belief now shown to be mistaken
emphasise how long the two friends have begged together
suggest that the Samanas never change their rules
C.explanation: "Always... I had thought" and "always I had believed" stress how fixed his view of Govinda was, a view Govinda's wish now overturns. It does not show Govinda always agrees, since Govinda now proposes something new. The Samanas' rules are not discussed. Begging together is not what the repeated word refers to; it refers to his belief.

C.prompt: Govinda's use of the phrase "the path of paths" most likely serves to
options: introduce a new teaching that Govinda has heard from a Brahmin in the village
show that Govinda has accepted Siddhartha's view
name a road that leads to the Buddha's grove
turn Siddhartha's own words back on him to dispute his claim
C.explanation: Siddhartha has just said "the path of paths, we will not find"; Govinda repeats the phrase to ask how "no one" could find it, using his friend's words to dispute him. It is not a new teaching. His protest against "terrible words" shows he has not accepted the view. The phrase is spiritual, not a real road.

C.prompt: Passage 2 most strongly suggests which outcome for the goal described in Passage 1?
options: The goal stays out of reach, since every escape ends in a return to the self.
The goal is fully reached, since his soul passes into thousands of other forms.
The goal changes, since Siddhartha now seeks only bodily strength.
The goal is abandoned, since Siddhartha decides the self is good.
C.explanation: Passage 1 hopes the self will die so the innermost being can awake; Passage 2 shows him awaking "every time to find his old self again," so the goal stays out of reach. Passing into many forms is not the hoped-for awakening. He does not decide the self is good here. Bodily strength is never his aim in either passage.

C.prompt: How does Govinda's reminder in Passage 2 relate to Siddhartha's questions in Passage 1?
options: It shows that Govinda was the first to doubt the Samanas.
It recalls the same doubt about the Samana path that Passage 1 shows him voicing.
It answers his questions by proving that both of them are now very near salvation.
It reveals that Siddhartha never questioned the path at all.
C.explanation: Passage 1 shows Siddhartha asking if they are "on the right path"; in Passage 2 Govinda recalls him saying he "would not walk the path of the Samanas for much longer," the same doubt. Govinda proves nothing about salvation. Siddhartha, not Govinda, voiced the doubt first. Passage 1 itself shows him questioning, so "never questioned" is wrong.
